Warm-up: Phone screen time is a safe confession. Take four answers, then move on.
The lesson is about future forms, not about how much anybody uses their phone.
Vocabulary: Go online, log on, switch off, get in touch are learned as units.
It means both turning a device off and stopping thinking about work. Both appear in the recording.
Grammar: Is it a plan in your head, or is it in the diary with another person? That is the whole distinction.
Do not pretend one is wrong when both work. Say which sounds more natural and why.
The recognition task is on going to reduced to /gənə/. Recognition only — do not drill it.
Practice: Exercise 1 is the one that carries the lesson. Give it time.
Exercise 6 brings back verb + -ing / verb + to from Lesson 10. Name it as recycling.
Listening: Three plays: gist, then part 1, then parts 2 and 3. Do not translate.
Three parts, three times of day
Morning, the working day, and ten at night. Use the part buttons rather than replaying the whole thing.
4.10 is one short task only. Two plays at most.
Now you: Insist they use their actual week. Invented arrangements produce invented English.
One future form used well, one to try again.
Wrap: The verb patterns came back today, in Practice 6 and inside plan to and look forward to.
Lesson 12 turns the plan into an actual invitation.

Stage 3 · Grammar

going to, and the Present Continuous

Both are the future. One is in your head, the other is in the diary.

Read these four sentences from the recording.
  • Today, I’m going to spend 24 hours without the internet.
  • This morning I’m visiting a fashion show with colleagues.
  • Then I’m meeting a friend for lunch at one o’clock.
  • I’m going to look through some magazines this afternoon.
Some are already arranged with another person, at a fixed time. Which form do they use?
In your head, or in the diary?
going to — an intentionPresent Continuous — an arrangement
What it meansyou have decided, but nothing is fixed with anybody elsea time, a place and usually another person are already fixed
PositiveI’m going to look through some magazines.I’m meeting a friend at one o’clock.
NegativeI’m not going to deal with work emails.I’m not working on Friday.
QuestionWhat are you going to do first?Are you doing anything on Friday night?
Short answerYes, I am. / No, I’m not.Yes, I am. / No, I’m not.
Time wordsone day · soon · this year · in futuretonight · tomorrow · on Friday · at one o’clock · next week
Also going tofor something you can already see coming: Look at those clouds — it’s going to rain.
Not the same as willWill is a prediction with no plan behind it. Going to and the Present Continuous both mean somebody has already decided something.

THE QUESTION TO ASK. Is it only in your head, or is it in the diary with somebody else? In your head → going to. In the diary → Present Continuous.

BOTH ARE OFTEN FINE. I’m going to see my sister later and I’m seeing my sister later are both correct. The second one sounds more fixed.

The mistake to watch: the Present Simple is not a future form here. I meet a friend tomorrow is wrong; say I’m meeting a friend tomorrow.

GOING TO = AN INTENTION. You have decided to do something, but nothing is fixed with anybody else: I’m going to look through some magazines this afternoon. Form: am / is / are + going to + the plain verb.

PRESENT CONTINUOUS = AN ARRANGEMENT. A time, a place and usually another person are already fixed: I’m meeting a friend for lunch at one o’clock. Form: am / is / are + -ing, exactly as in the present, with a future time word.

OFTEN BOTH WORK. I’m going to see my sister later and I’m seeing my sister later are both correct English. The Present Continuous sounds more definite, as though it is written down somewhere.

GOING TO FOR EVIDENCE. There is a second use: something you can already see coming. Look at those clouds — it’s going to rain. Nobody has decided anything; the evidence is in front of you.

Two mistakes to watch: the Present Simple is not a future form (I meet a friend tomorrow is wrong), and going to go is correct but heavy — I’m going to Paris is what people actually say.

In Lesson 12 you will use both of these to invite somebody and to say when you are free.

Full grammar reference — going to and the Present Continuous for the future

Form

going toI’m going to learn Spanish. · He isn’t going to come.
QuestionAre you going to apply? · What are you going to do?
Present ContinuousI’m meeting Aigerim on Friday. · We’re not flying until Sunday.
Short answersYes, I am. / No, he isn’t.
Both use beam / is / are — so the negative and the question are made with be.

When and why we use it

  • going to = an intention decided before now: I’m going to stop using social media.
  • going to also makes a prediction when you can see the evidence: Look at that sky — it’s going to rain.
  • Present Continuous = a fixed arrangement, usually with another person, and usually with a time and a place: I’m seeing the doctor at four.
  • In speech, going to is often gonna. Understand it; write the full form.

Signal words

tonight · tomorrow · next week · on Friday · at the weekend · in June

Watch out — the mistakes learners really make

  • I’m going to walking. → I’m going to walk.After going to, the plain verb.
  • I meet a friend tomorrow. → I’m meeting a friend tomorrow.An arrangement takes the continuous.
  • I will meet Aigerim — it’s arranged. → I’m meeting Aigerim.Will is not used for arrangements.
  • I’m going to the cinema tonight going to. → I’m going to the cinema tonight.go does not need going to go.

Don’t confuse it with

going to = the plan is in your head. Present Continuous = it is in the diary. Will (Unit 7) = you decide as you speak.
